A UX flow tells you **what** a product must do: which screens exist and how a person moves between them. A wireframe shows the rough layout in grey boxes. **UI design** turns that into the exact interface a developer will build: real colours, real fonts, exact spacing in pixels, every button state, and a clickable prototype. This course assumes you already understand basic UX ideas (users, flows, wireframes). Here we focus on the craft of building the interface itself in Figma, to a standard that holds up when a developer opens the file.

Figma is a design tool that runs in a web browser, with desktop apps for Windows and macOS and a mobile app for viewing designs and prototypes on a phone. Because files live online, a client in Lagos, a developer in Nairobi and you in Abuja can open the same file at the same time and see each other's cursors. That is the main reason teams use it: one shared source of truth instead of screenshots sent back and forth on WhatsApp.

Constraints: pinning elements to edges

Select a layer inside a frame and the Constraints section shows horizontal options (Left, Right, Left and right, Center, Scale) and vertical options (Top, Bottom, Top and bottom, Center, Scale). A cart icon in the top right corner should be **Right** and **Top**, so it stays in the corner when the screen widens. A search bar should be **Left and right**, so it stretches. A bottom navigation bar should be **Left and right** plus **Bottom**. Test by dragging the edge of the frame: whatever moves wrongly needs a different constraint.
Auto layout: the core professional skill

Auto layout turns a frame into a flexible stack, similar to how a web developer lays out a page with CSS flexbox. You choose a **direction** (vertical, horizontal or wrap), a **gap** between items, **padding** around the inside edges and **alignment**. Each child, and the frame itself, then gets a resizing rule:
**Hug contents**: the frame shrinks or grows to fit what is inside. A button that hugs its label grows when "Add" becomes "Add to cart".
**Fill container**: the child stretches to take the space its parent gives it. A product card's text column fills the width beside the image.
**Fixed**: an exact size that does not change, such as a 64 × 64 product photo.
Text layers also have **Auto width**, **Auto height**, **Fixed size** and **Truncate text**; long product names in a card usually need Auto height or Truncate with a maximum number of lines.

Layout grids

A **layout grid** draws guide columns on a frame so content lines up across screens. Polished interfaces feel calm because they repeat a small number of decisions. Professionals do not choose spacing, font sizes and colours screen by screen. They define **foundations** once and use them everywhere. In this lesson you set those foundations for Oja Fresh on the Foundations page of your file.
A person choosing colours from a palette
Foundations such as colour roles, spacing and type are decided once and then reused across every screen.
Spacing on an 8-point system

Most product teams use an **8-point system**: spacing and sizes are multiples of 8, with 4 allowed for small gaps. A typical approved set is **4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48**. Inside a card you might use 12 padding and 4 or 8 between lines of text; between sections of a screen, 24 or 32. Because only these values are allowed, screens line up and developers can turn them into a short list of spacing tokens. Multiples of 4 and 8 also convert to whole pixels at 1.5x, 2x and 3x screen densities, which keeps edges crisp.
A type scale you can explain

A **type scale** is a short ladder of text sizes made by multiplying a base size by a fixed ratio. Body text on mobile is usually 16 to 17: Material Design's main body style is 16, and Apple's default body text is 17 points. We will use 16. With a ratio of 1.25 (called a major third) each step is 25 percent larger than the one below it.

Designing for real conditions
**Small screens**: test every screen at 360 px wide. Keep tap targets at least 48 × 48 (Android guidance) or 44 × 44 points (Apple guidance).
**Bright sunlight**: users often check orders outdoors. Strong contrast and 16 px body text help far more than thin, pale grey text.
**Data cost**: every large photo costs the user money to load. Design layouts that still make sense with small thumbnails or a plain placeholder colour while images load.

**Local text**: test real words, not filler text. Yoruba and Igbo use tone marks (for example "ẹ̀fọ́"), Hausa uses hooked letters (ɓ, ɗ, ƙ), and English labels may be translated later and grow longer. Make sure your font supports the characters you need and that buttons hug their labels.
**Money formatting**: show naira as "₦6,500" with the naira sign and a thousands comma, and agree the format with the developer.

You turn your foundations into a reusable component library, connect your screens into a prototype a client can tap through on a phone, and run the quality checks and handoff steps that let a developer build your design without guessing.

A **component** is an element you build once and reuse: a button, an input field, a product card, a bottom navigation bar. The original is the **main component** (purple diamond icon in the layers panel). Every copy is an **instance**. Change the main component and every instance updates across the file. In an instance you can still **override** some things, such as the label text or an icon, without breaking the link. This is what lets one designer keep 40 screens consistent.
Interface components arranged as reusable building blocks
A component library is a set of building blocks: build each piece once, reuse it on every screen.
Tools and setup for this stage

**Plan**: the free Starter plan is enough to learn and build a portfolio. Paid plans add things such as unlimited shared files, team libraries and Dev Mode. Students and teachers can apply for the free Education plan. Check figma.com/pricing for current limits before you promise a client anything that depends on a paid feature.
**Desktop app**: lighter on browser memory and lets you use fonts installed on your computer. The browser works too.

**Community kits**: Google's Material 3 Design Kit and Apple's iOS UI kits are published on the Figma Community. Study how they name and structure components; do not ship them unchanged as your own work.

**Plugins** (Main menu, Plugins): a contrast checker, an icon plugin such as Iconify, and a stock photo plugin such as Unsplash cover most needs. Install only plugins from known publishers and never paste client passwords or private data into a plugin.
From element to component set
Build the element with auto layout and your saved styles only (no loose colours).
Select it and press Ctrl + Alt + K (Mac: Cmd + Option + K). Name it with a slash path, for example "Button".
Duplicate the main component for each version you need, select all of them and click **Combine as variants**. Figma wraps them in a dashed purple **component set**.
In the right panel, rename the default property "Property 1" to something meaningful, such as **Type**, and give each value a clear name: Primary, Secondary, Ghost.
Add more variant properties only when the look truly changes, for example **State** (Default, Pressed, Disabled) and **Size** (Medium, Large).
Use the other property types to avoid duplicating variants: **Text** (edit the label from the panel), **Boolean** (show or hide an icon), **Instance swap** (choose which icon).
Worked example: keeping the button set small
For example, Amaka needs Oja Fresh buttons in 3 types, 3 states and 2 sizes, and some buttons need a leading icon (a cart or a plus sign).
Variants needed without icons: 3 types × 3 states × 2 sizes = 18 variants.
If she made "with icon" a variant too, the count doubles: 18 × 2 = 36 variants, and every future change must be made 36 times over.
Instead she puts an icon instance in every variant and adds a **Boolean** property "Show icon" linked to the icon layer's visibility. The count stays at 18.
She adds an **Instance swap** property "Icon" so a designer can choose cart, plus or arrow from the panel without detaching.
She adds a **Text** property "Label" linked to the text layer, so the label is edited from the right panel.
She tests: places an instance on the Home screen, switches Type to Secondary, turns Show icon on, swaps the icon to plus and types "Add to cart". The button hugs the longer label.

Put all main components on the **Components** page, grouped in sections: Actions (buttons, icon buttons), Inputs (text field, dropdown, checkbox), Display (product card, badge, price tag), Navigation (top bar, bottom nav, tabs). Detaching is a last resort

Detach instance (Ctrl + Alt + B, Mac Cmd + Option + B) breaks the link to the main component. The detached copy will never receive future fixes. If you keep wanting to detach, your component is missing a property or a variant; fix the component instead.
Variables for modes and tokens

Figma **variables** store reusable values of four types: colour, number, string and boolean. A collection can have **modes**, for example Light and Dark, so the same variable "Color/Surface" is white in Light and near-black in Dark. Number variables are ideal for spacing and radius tokens (Space/16, Radius/12). Developers can read these names in their code later, which is a big step towards a shared language between design and code. Check your plan's limits on how many modes you can create.

Scrolling and fixed elements

Phone screens scroll. Make the Home frame taller than the device if the content needs it, or keep the device height and let the content overflow with clipping on. Then set **vertical scrolling** for the frame (overflow behaviour). Select the top app bar and bottom navigation and set their position to **Fixed** (or **Sticky** for a header that scrolls up and then sticks) so they stay in place while the list moves. A prototype where the bottom navigation scrolls away looks broken to clients.
Smart Animate and interactive components

**Smart animate** looks for layers with the **same name** in the start and end frames and animates the differences in position, size, colour and opacity. If the cart badge is called "Badge" in both frames and its number changes from 1 to 2, it will animate smoothly. If one is called "Badge" and the other "Ellipse 3", it will just jump. Keep names identical.

**Interactive components** add behaviour inside a component set. In your Button set, connect the Default variant to the Pressed variant with While pressing, Change to. Every instance in every screen now shows the pressed state automatically. The same works for checkboxes (On tap, Change to Checked) and favourite icons.

Colour contrast: the numbers

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2) set minimum **contrast ratios** for level AA, the level most organisations aim for: **4.5 : 1** for normal text, **3 : 1** for large text (about 24 px regular or 18.7 px bold and above), and **3 : 1** for important non-text parts such as input borders and icons that carry meaning. The ratio is (L1 + 0.05) ÷ (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the relative luminance of the lighter colour and L2 of the darker. White has luminance 1.
Worked example: auditing four Oja Fresh colour pairs
For example, before handover Amaka checks the pairs used most on her screens with a contrast checker plugin, and confirms one by hand.
By hand: grey #757575 has relative luminance of about 0.178. On white: (1 + 0.05) ÷ (0.178 + 0.05) = 1.05 ÷ 0.228 = about 4.6 : 1. Passes 4.5 for normal text, just.
Same grey on her light card background #F5F5F5: the plugin shows about 4.2 : 1. Fails for normal text. She switches secondary text to #616161, about 6.2 : 1 on white.
White text on the green primary button #2E7D32: about 5.1 : 1. Passes.
White text on an orange promo tag #EF6C00: about 3.1 : 1. Fails for 13 px text. She darkens it to #BF360C, about 5.6 : 1.
Input border #BDBDBD on white: about 1.9 : 1. Fails the 3 : 1 non-text rule, so users may not see where to type. She darkens the border to #757575.
Three of five pairs needed fixing. Each fix took one edit to a colour variable, and every screen updated at once.
Same colour, different result
Contrast depends on both colours. A grey that passes on white can fail on light grey. Always check text against the actual background it sits on.

**Tap targets**: interactive areas at least 48 × 48 on Android (44 × 44 points on iOS). An icon can be 24 px if its tappable frame is 48. WCAG 2.2 also sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels at AA.
**Text resizing**: increase body text by 30 percent on a test copy of one screen. Do buttons and cards grow without overlapping? Auto layout with Hug makes this pass.
**States**: every input has Default, Focused, Filled, Error and Disabled; every list has an empty state; every data screen has loading and error states.
**Not colour alone**: an error is shown by colour plus an icon and a message, so colour-blind users still see it.
**Consistency**: Figma's Selection colors section shows every colour used in a selection; anything not linked to a style or variable is a stray to fix.

Terms that control scope
**Included**: list every screen by name, the platforms, the components and the deliverables (Figma file, prototype link, spec page, exported assets).
**Revision rounds**: for example, two rounds of consolidated feedback per stage. A round is one written list from the named decision-maker.
**Change requests**: new screens or features are quoted with the same weights. A new medium screen in this example is 5 h × ₦10,000 = ₦50,000.

Core skill
Manual frame or auto layout?
Auto layout
A beginner's screen looks fine at one size and breaks at every other. With a manual frame, you move each item by hand, and longer text overlaps.
Auto layout, Shift plus A, turns a frame into a flexible stack. You choose a direction, a gap between items, and padding inside. New items slot in, and spacing stays the same everywhere.
Resizing rules
Hug, Fill or Fixed
The frame fits what is inside. A button grows when Add becomes Add to cart.
The child stretches to the space its parent gives it, like a card's text column.
An exact size that does not change, such as a 64 × 64 product photo.
Each element gets a resizing rule. Hug contents means the frame fits what is inside, so a button grows with its label.
Fill container means it stretches to take the space its parent gives it.
Fixed means an exact size, like a 64 by 64 product photo.

Why this matters
Build once, reuse everywhere
Main component: the original
Instances: copies that stay linked
Overrides: change a label, keep the link
One designer, 40 consistent screens
A component is an element you build once and reuse, like a button or a product card. The original is the main component.
Every copy is an instance. Change the main component, and every instance updates. In an instance you can still override things like the label, without breaking the link.
This is what lets one designer keep 40 screens consistent.
Step by step
Build with auto layout and saved styles
Ctrl + Alt + K to create the component
Duplicate, then Combine as variants
Rename Property 1 to Type, State, Size
Add text, boolean, instance swap props
Do not detach. If you want to, fix the component instead.
Build the element with auto layout and only your saved styles. Then press Control, Alt, K, or Command, Option, K on a Mac, to make it a component.
Duplicate it for each version you need, select them all, and click Combine as variants.
Rename the default Property 1 to something meaningful, like Type, with values such as Primary and Secondary.
Then add other properties: Text to edit the label, Boolean to show or hide an icon, and Instance swap to choose which icon.
Detaching an instance breaks its link forever, so it never receives future fixes. If you keep wanting to detach, your component is missing a property.
Worked example
Keep the button set small
Icon as a variant
3 types × 3 states × 2 sizes = 18
Double it for icons: 36
Every change made 36 times
Icon as a property
Still 18 variants
Boolean: Show icon
Instance swap: cart, plus, arrow
Text property: the label
Amaka needs buttons in 3 types, 3 states and 2 sizes. That is 18 variants. If she made the icon a variant too, the count doubles to 36, and every future change must be made 36 times.
Instead she adds a Boolean property, Show icon, an Instance swap property for the icon, and a Text property for the label. The set stays at 18 variants and covers every button in the app.
Prototypes
Every connection has four parts
Trigger: what the user does
Action: what happens
Destination: where it goes
Animation: how it moves
A prototype links your screens so a client can tap through them before paying for development. Each connection has a trigger, like On tap, and an action, like Navigate to or Open overlay.
Then a destination frame, and an animation. Around 200 to 300 ms, with ease out, suits most mobile transitions.

Fixed bars on scrolling screens

Ask about brand: is there a logo, colours, fonts? And users: what are the three most important things they do, and has anyone mapped the flows?

Red flags
Hidden scope to price separately
Just make it like a big company's app
We will send the content later
Phone, tablet and web
Can you also do the logo?
No named decision-maker
Watch for red flags. Make it like a big company's app means dozens of screens, so ask which three matter most. Content later means sample content, with replacing it as a separate task.
Each extra platform multiplies screens. A logo is a separate project. And no named decision-maker means endless feedback, unless you set limits.
Pricing
Build the estimate from the screens
Simple screen: about 3 hours
Medium screen: about 5 hours
Complex screen: about 8 hours
Add components, prototype, handoff
Add a 10 to 20 percent buffer
Weight each screen by effort. As a starting scale, a simple screen is about 3 hours, a medium one about 5, and a complex form or checkout about 8. Track your own time to make these honest.
Then add the work that is not screens: foundations and components, the prototype, and handoff.
Add a buffer for unknowns. Kemi's app comes to 91 hours, plus 15 percent, about 105 hours.
For example, 105 hours at an illustrative 10,000 naira per hour for Kemi's app.
Deposit, 50 percent
Key screens approved, 30 percent
At handoff, 20 percent
Illustrative naira rate, not a market figure.
At an example rate of 10,000 naira an hour, 105 hours is 1,050,000 naira. Set your own rate from your costs, skill and local demand.
Split it by milestone: a 50 percent deposit of 525,000 naira, 30 percent when key screens are approved, and 20 percent at handoff.

Write the limits too: two rounds of feedback per stage, and a price for each new screen. A new medium screen here is 50,000 naira. If the client wants to save money, remove a line, not just the total.

Scams aimed at freelancers
A client sends more than agreed and asks for a refund. Be wary.
A screenshot or SMS alert is not money. Confirm it in your bank or wallet app.
Never share your BVN, OTPs or PIN. Share view-only links until final payment.
Protect your money. Be wary of a new client who sends more than agreed and asks you to refund the difference.
A payment screenshot or SMS alert is not money. Confirm every payment inside your own bank or wallet app before you start or deliver.
Never share your BVN, OTPs or banking PIN. And keep the file in your own Figma team, sharing view-only links, until the final payment.
